{{Short description|Algebraic structure}}
In mathematics, a [[Lie algebra]] has been generalized in several ways.

== Graded Lie algebra and Lie superalgebra ==
{{main|graded Lie algebra|Lie superalgebra}}

A graded Lie algebra is a Lie algebra with grading. When the grading is <math>\mathbb{Z}/2</math>, it is also known as a Lie superalgebra.

== Lie-isotopic algebra ==
A '''Lie-isotopic algebra''' is a generalization of Lie algebras proposed by physicist R. M. Santilli in 1978.

=== Definition ===
Recall that a finite-dimensional [[Lie algebra]]<ref>{{Citation | last=Trell |first=Erik | title=English Translation of Marius Sophus Lie' Doctoral Thesis |  year=1998 | journal=[[Algebras, Groups and Geometries]] | issn=0741-9937 | volume=15 | issue=4 | pages=395–446 |url=http://www.santilli-foundation.org/docs/Santilli-54.pdf  }}</ref> <math>L</math>  with generators <math>X_1, X_2, ..., X_n</math> and commutation rules

:<math> [X_i X_j] = X_i X_j - X_j X_i = C_{ij}^k X_k,</math>

can be defined (particularly in physics) as the totally anti-symmetric algebra <math>A(L)^-</math> attached to the universal enveloping associative algebra <math>A(L)=\{X_1, X_2, ..., X_n; X_iX_j, i, j = 1, ..., n; 1\}</math> equipped with the associative product <math>X_i \times X_j</math> over a numeric field <math>F</math> with multiplicative unit <math>1</math>.

Consider now the axiom-preserving lifting of <math>A(L)</math> into the form <math>A^*(L^*)=\{X_1, X_2, ..., X_n; X_i\times X_j, i, j = 1, ..., n; 1^*\}</math>, called [[universal enveloping isoassociative algebra,]]<ref>Sect. 5.2, p. 154 on of {{cite book |last=Santilli | first= Ruggero M. |title=Foundation of Theoretical Mechanics |volume=II |publisher=Springer Verlag |year=1983 |isbn=3-540-09482-2 |url=http://www.santilli-foundation.org/docs/santilli-69.pdf}}</ref> with isoproduct

:<math>X_i\times X_j = X_i T^* X_j, </math>

verifying the [[isoassociative law]]

:<math>X_i\times (X_j  \times X_k) = X_i\times (X_j \times X_k)  </math>

and multiplicative [[isounit]]

:<math>1^* = 1/T*,  1^* \times X_k = X_k \times 1^* = X_k \forall  X_k  in A^*(L^*)</math>

where <math>T^*</math>, called the [[isotopic element]], is not necessarily an element of <math>A(L)</math> which is solely restricted by the condition of being positive-definite, <math>T^* > 0</math> , but otherwise having any desired dependence on local variables, and the products <math>X_i T^*, T^* X_j, etc.</math> are conventional associative products in <math>A(L)</math>.

Then a Lie-isotopic algebra<ref>Sect.5.3, p. 163 on of {{cite book |last=Santilli | first= Ruggero M. |title=Foundation of Theoretical Mechanics |volume=II |publisher=Springer Verlag |year=1983 |isbn=3-540-09482-2 |url=http://www.santilli-foundation.org/docs/santilli-69.pdf}}</ref> <math>L^*</math> can be defined as the totally antisymmetric algebra attached to the enveloping isoassociative algebra. <math>L^* = A^*(L^*)^-</math> with [[isocommutation rules]]

:<math> [X_i, X_j]^* = X_i \times X_j - X_j \times X_i = X_i T^* X_j - X_j T^* X_i = C_{ij}^{*k} X_k.</math>

It is evident that:<ref>Sect 5.4, p. 173 on of {{cite book |last=Santilli | first= Ruggero M. |title=Foundation of Theoretical Mechanics |volume=II |publisher=Springer Verlag |year=1983 |isbn=3-540-09482-2 |url=http://www.santilli-foundation.org/docs/santilli-69.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Sourlas | first=  Dimitris S. and Tsagas, Grigorious T. |title=Mathematical Foundation of the Lie-Santilli Theory |publisher=Ukraine Academy of Sciences |year= 1993 |isbn=0-911767-69-X  | url=http://www.santilli-foundation.org/docs/santilli-70.pdf}}</ref> 1) The isoproduct and the isounit coincide at the abstract level with the conventional product and; 2)  The isocommutators <math>[X_i, X_j]^*</math> verify Lie's axioms; 3) In view of the infinitely possible isotopic elements <math>T^*</math> (as numbers, functions, matrices, operators, etc.), any given Lie algebra <math>L</math> admits an infinite class of isotopes; 4) Lie-isotopic algebras are called<ref>{{Citation | last1=Muktibodh | first1=Arum S. |last2=Santilli |first2=Ruggero M. |  title=Studies of the Regular and Irregular Isorepresentations of the Lie-Santilli Isotheory |  year=2007 | journal=[[Journal of Generalized Lie Theories]] |volume=11 | pages=1–7 |url=http://www.santilli-foundation.org/docs/isorep-Lie-Santilli-2017.pdf }}</ref>  regular
whenever <math>C_{ij}^{*k} = C_{ij}^{k}</math>,  and irregular
whenever <math>C_{ij}^{*k} \ne C_{ij}^{k}</math>. 5) All regular Lie-isotope <math>L^*</math> are evidently isomorphic to <math>L</math>.  However, the relationship between irregular isotopes <math>L^*</math>  and <math>L</math> 
does not appear to have been studied to date (Jan. 20, 2024).

An illustration of the applications cf Lie-isotopic algebras in physics is given by the isotopes <math>SU^*(2)</math> of the <math>SU(2)</math>-spin symmetry 
<ref>{{Citation | last=Santilli |first=Ruggero M. |title=Isorepresentation of the Lie-isotopic $SU(2)$ Algebra with Application to Nuclear Physics and local realism |  year=1998 |journal=[[Acta Applicandae Mathematicae]] | issn=0741-9937 | volume=50 |  pages=177–190 |url=http://www.santilli-foundation.org/docs/Santilli-27.pdf}}</ref> whose fundamental representation on a Hilbert space <math>H</math>  over the field of complex numbers <math>C</math> can be obtained via the nonunitary transformation of the fundamental reopreserntation of <math>SU(2)</math> (Pauli matrices)

:<math>
\sigma^*_k =  U \sigma_k U^\dagger,</math>

:<math>
U U^\dagger = 
I ^* = Diag. (\lambda^{-1}, \lambda), Det 1^* = 1,</math>

:<math>
 \sigma^*_1= \left(\!
\begin{array}{cc}
0& \lambda\\
\lambda^{-1}& 0
\end{array}
\!\right),    
 \sigma^*_2 = \left(\!
\begin{array}{cc}
0& -i\! \lambda\\
i\! \lambda^{-1}& 0
\end{array}
\!\right),   
\sigma^*_3 = \left(\!
\begin{array}{cc}
\lambda^{-1}& 0\\
0&  -\lambda
\end{array}
\!\right ),
</math>

providing an explicit and concrete realization of [[Bohm's hidden variables]] <math>\lambda</math>,<ref>{{Citation | last=Bohm |first=David | title=A Suggested Interpretation of the Quantum Theory in Terms of 'Hidden Variables' |  year=1952 | journal=[[Phys. Rev.]] | volume=85 |  pages=166–182 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.85.166 |url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.85.166}}</ref> which is 'hidden' in the abstract axiom of associativity and allows an exact representation of the Deuteron magnetic moment.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Sanrtilli | first1=Ruggero M. |last2=Sobczyk |first2=Garret |  title=Representation of nuclear magnetic moments via a Clifford algebra formulation of Bohm's hidden variables |  year=2022 | journal=[[Scientific Reports]] |volume=12 | issue=1 | pages=1–10 | doi=10.1038/s41598-022-24970-4  | doi-access=free| pmid=36529817 | pmc=9760646 | bibcode=2022NatSR..1220674S |url=https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-24970-4}}</ref>

== Quasi-Lie algebra ==
A '''quasi-Lie algebra''' in [[abstract algebra]] is just like a [[Lie algebra]], but with the usual [[axiom]]

:<math>[x,x]=0</math>

replaced by

:<math>[x,y]=-[y,x]</math> (anti-symmetry).

In [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] other than 2, these are equivalent (in the presence of [[bilinear operator|bilinearity]]), so this distinction doesn't arise when considering real or complex Lie algebras. It can however become important, when considering ''Lie algebras'' over the integers.

In a quasi-Lie algebra,

:<math>2[x,x]=0.</math>

Therefore, the bracket of any element with itself is 2-torsion, if it does not actually vanish.

See also: [[Whitehead product]].
